questions.q: What is an object-oriented database?
options: A database that stores data as objects with identity, state and behavior
A database that stores only flat text files
A database that cannot represent complex data
A database that uses only hash buckets
questions.explanation: Object-oriented databases model persistent data using object-oriented concepts such as objects, classes and inheritance.

questions.q: What is object identity in an object-oriented database?
options: The object's current attribute value
A unique identity that distinguishes an object independently of its attribute values
The name of the database server
The number of indexes on the object
questions.explanation: Object identity distinguishes objects even when two objects have identical attribute values.

questions.q: What is encapsulation?
options: Storing every attribute in a separate database
Combining all tables into one table
Bundling data with the operations that manipulate it and controlling access to internal details
Removing object methods
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation details and exposes an object's behavior through defined interfaces.

questions.q: What is inheritance in an object-oriented data model?
options: A transaction copying a lock
A table referencing itself
A query using a subquery
A subclass acquiring properties and behavior from a superclass
questions.explanation: Inheritance supports reuse and specialization by allowing subclasses to inherit from parent classes.

questions.q: What is polymorphism?
options: The ability to use a common interface with different implementations for different object types
The ability to store only one data type
A rule that all objects must have identical values
A method for encrypting records
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets the same operation or interface behave differently for different object classes.

questions.q: What is a persistent object?
options: An object that exists only during one expression
An object whose state is stored beyond the lifetime of the program that created it
An object that cannot be updated
An object without identity
questions.explanation: Persistence allows objects to survive program termination by storing their state in durable storage.

questions.q: What is an object-relational database?
options: A database that supports only object files
A database without SQL
A relational database extended with object-oriented features and richer data types
A database that stores no structured data
questions.explanation: Object-relational systems retain relational tables and add features such as user-defined types, collections or inheritance-like capabilities.

questions.q: Which feature is commonly associated with object-relational databases?
options: Only fixed-length character fields
No support for constraints
No support for SQL
User-defined types
questions.explanation: Object-relational DBMSs may allow users to define structured types beyond basic built-in types.

questions.q: What is a user-defined type (UDT)?
options: A type created by a database designer to represent application-specific data
A type that can store only NULL
A database backup format
A transaction isolation level
questions.explanation: UDTs let database schemas model structured or specialized values that are meaningful to an application.

questions.q: What is a collection type in an object-relational database?
options: A type that stores only one integer
A type that can represent a group of values, such as an array or nested collection
A type used only for passwords
A type that replaces every relation
questions.explanation: Collection types represent multiple related values as a single structured attribute or value, depending on DBMS support.

questions.q: What is a logical database?
options: A physical disk partition
A database stored only on a web browser
A database representation organized around logical data structures rather than physical storage details
A transaction log
questions.explanation: The logical view describes data organization and relationships without specifying exactly how bytes are stored on disk.

questions.q: What does a logical data model describe?
options: The exact physical sector number of each row
The brand of storage device
The CPU instruction set
Entities, attributes, relationships and constraints relevant to the data
questions.explanation: A logical model represents the data requirements and structure independently of low-level storage details.

questions.q: What is a physical data model concerned with?
options: How data is implemented and stored, including tables, indexes and storage details
Only business vocabulary
Only user interface colors
Only the names of application users
questions.explanation: A physical model describes implementation choices such as data types, indexes, partitions and storage organization.

questions.q: What is a web database application?
options: A database that can only be accessed by a local keyboard
An application in which a web interface communicates with a database through an application or server layer
A database without users
A database that stores only HTML files
questions.explanation: A web application commonly sends requests to a server, which applies application logic and queries the database.

questions.q: Why should a web browser generally not connect directly to a database using privileged credentials?
options: Browsers cannot display tables
It makes SQL syntax invalid
It exposes credentials and bypasses important server-side controls
It prevents HTML from loading
questions.explanation: A server-side layer protects credentials, validates requests and enforces authorization before database access.

questions.q: What is the role of an application server in a web database system?
options: To replace the database with a monitor
To store only browser history
To provide network cabling
To process client requests and coordinate application logic and database operations
questions.explanation: The application server mediates between clients and the database, applying business rules and security checks.

questions.q: What is a three-tier web architecture?
options: Presentation tier, application tier and data tier
Three database tables with the same name
Three copies of each password
Three indexes on every column
questions.explanation: Three-tier architecture separates the user interface, application logic and data management responsibilities.

questions.q: What is the presentation tier responsible for?
options: Managing disk page replacement
Displaying information and accepting user interaction
Enforcing B-tree split rules
Writing transaction log records
questions.explanation: The presentation tier is the user-facing layer through which people interact with the application.

questions.q: What is the data tier responsible for?
options: Rendering web pages
Validating button colors
Storing and retrieving persistent application data
Managing browser tabs
questions.explanation: The data tier manages persistence, commonly through a database management system.

questions.q: What is a distributed database?
options: A database stored in one table only
A database with no network communication
A collection of unrelated spreadsheets
A logically related database whose data is stored across multiple networked sites
questions.explanation: A distributed database presents a unified data system even though data is physically located at multiple sites.

questions.q: What is a distributed DBMS?
options: Software that manages a distributed database and coordinates access across sites
A tool used only to draw ER diagrams
A local text editor
A program that only compresses files
questions.explanation: A distributed DBMS coordinates data storage, queries, transactions and other database functions across sites.

questions.q: What is data fragmentation in a distributed database?
options: Encrypting every relation
Dividing a relation into smaller pieces for storage at different sites
Deleting duplicate users
Combining all indexes into one
questions.explanation: Fragmentation partitions data into pieces that can be placed at different locations.

questions.q: What is horizontal fragmentation?
options: Splitting a relation by columns
Copying the database log
Dividing a relation into subsets of rows
Converting a table into an object
questions.explanation: Horizontal fragmentation divides tuples according to predicates, with each fragment containing selected rows.

questions.q: What is vertical fragmentation?
options: Dividing a relation into subsets of rows
Sorting rows by primary key
Replicating every page
Dividing a relation into subsets of columns, typically retaining a key for reconstruction
questions.explanation: Vertical fragmentation separates attributes into groups and uses a common key to reconstruct the original relation.

questions.q: What is replication in a distributed database?
options: Maintaining copies of data at multiple sites
Splitting one column into smaller values
Removing all remote access
Replacing tables with views
questions.explanation: Replication stores copies of data at multiple locations to improve availability or read performance.

questions.q: What is one potential disadvantage of replication?
options: It makes all data disappear
Updates must be coordinated to keep copies consistent
It prevents read operations
It eliminates network traffic
questions.explanation: Replicated copies can become inconsistent unless updates are propagated and coordinated correctly.

questions.q: What is data transparency in a distributed DBMS?
options: Users must manually locate every disk sector
Users must write a separate query for every copy
The system hides certain distribution details from users and applications
The system reveals all passwords
questions.explanation: Transparency makes distributed data appear more unified by hiding details such as location or fragmentation.

questions.q: What is location transparency?
options: Users must know each fragment's physical address
All data must be stored at one site
Every query must specify a server name
Users can access data without knowing the site where it is physically stored
questions.explanation: Location transparency hides the physical site or network location of data from the user.

questions.q: What is fragmentation transparency?
options: Users can query a relation without knowing how it has been divided into fragments
Users must combine every fragment manually
Users must know the disk format
Users can access only one fragment
questions.explanation: Fragmentation transparency hides the distribution of a relation into horizontal or vertical fragments.

questions.q: What is replication transparency?
options: Users must choose a replica for every read
The system hides the existence of multiple copies from users
The system prevents copies from being updated
The system stores only one copy
questions.explanation: Replication transparency lets users work with logical data without managing which replica is used.

questions.q: What is a distributed transaction?
options: A transaction that accesses only a local variable
A transaction that cannot commit
A transaction whose operations may involve data at more than one site
A transaction that has no read or write operations
questions.explanation: A distributed transaction coordinates work across multiple database sites and must handle failures and consistency.

questions.q: What is the purpose of two-phase commit (2PC)?
options: To balance a B-tree
To encrypt communication
To divide a relation vertically
To coordinate an atomic commit decision among distributed participants
questions.explanation: 2PC uses prepare and decision phases so participants can agree to commit or abort a distributed transaction.

questions.q: Which are the two main phases of two-phase commit?
options: Prepare (voting) and commit/abort decision
Read and write
Parse and optimize
Fragment and replicate
questions.explanation: The coordinator first asks participants to prepare and vote, then communicates the final commit or abort decision.

questions.q: What is a coordinator's role in 2PC?
options: To store every user's password
To initiate the protocol, collect participant votes and communicate the decision
To create all indexes
To split every relation into columns
questions.explanation: The coordinator manages the protocol and determines the global outcome from participant responses.

questions.q: What is a potential drawback of two-phase commit?
options: It never uses network messages
It permits participants to decide independently
Participants may remain blocked while waiting for the coordinator or a final decision
It cannot support distributed transactions
questions.explanation: 2PC can block if failures occur after participants prepare but before they learn the final outcome.

questions.q: What is a distributed query?
options: A query that can access only one local variable
A query that never reads data
A query that always deletes records
A query whose execution may access data stored at multiple sites
questions.explanation: A distributed query plan coordinates operations over data located at different networked sites.

questions.q: Why is query optimization important in a distributed database?
options: Communication cost and data transfer can be significant
Network bandwidth is always unlimited
Every site has identical data
Queries cannot use indexes
questions.explanation: Reducing data transferred across the network can substantially improve distributed query performance.

questions.q: What is a distributed database's site?
options: A SQL aggregate function
A computer or node participating in the distributed system
A column constraint
A B-tree leaf pointer
questions.explanation: A site is a location or node that stores data or provides processing in the distributed database.

questions.q: What is a homogeneous distributed database system?
options: A system with unrelated DBMS products at every site
A system with no shared schema
A system in which participating sites use the same DBMS software or data model
A system that stores data only on paper
questions.explanation: Homogeneous systems use a common DBMS environment across participating sites.

questions.q: What is a heterogeneous distributed database system?
options: A system in which every site must use identical DBMS software
A system with no network
A system with one local table
A system in which sites may use different DBMS products, data models or schemas
questions.explanation: Heterogeneous systems integrate sites with different database technologies or representations.

questions.q: What is a federated database system?
options: A system that provides integrated access to multiple autonomous databases
A single table with no constraints
A database that stores only images
A system that disables remote queries
questions.explanation: A federation provides a unified access layer while participating databases may retain some autonomy.

questions.q: What does database autonomy mean in a federated system?
options: All sites must be controlled by one application
A participating database can retain control over its local operations and data
Every site must share the same password
No site can change its schema
questions.explanation: Autonomy means local databases retain some independence in administration and operation.

questions.q: What is a cloud database?
options: A database that can exist only without a network
A database stored exclusively on a personal USB drive
A database service hosted on cloud infrastructure and accessed over a network
A database without backup support
questions.explanation: Cloud databases run on provider-managed or cloud-hosted infrastructure and are accessed through network services.

questions.q: What is database scalability?
options: The ability to remove all constraints
The ability to use only one user account
The ability to run without storage
The ability to handle increased workload by adding or using resources effectively
questions.explanation: Scalability describes how a system accommodates growth in users, data volume or request rate.

questions.q: What is horizontal scaling?
options: Adding more machines or nodes to share the workload
Increasing only the RAM of one machine
Reducing the number of database replicas
Removing the application server
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling adds nodes to distribute processing or storage across multiple machines.

questions.q: What is vertical scaling?
options: Adding many independent database sites
Increasing resources such as CPU, RAM or storage on a single machine
Splitting a table into rows
Creating more user roles
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling increases the capacity of an individual server by adding or upgrading its resources.

questions.q: What is a key concern in distributed database design?
options: Choosing a website font
Avoiding all indexes
Balancing data placement, availability, consistency and communication costs
Removing transaction management
questions.explanation: Distributed design must consider where data resides, how copies stay consistent and how sites communicate.

questions.q: What is schema integration in a heterogeneous distributed database?
options: Deleting all local schemas
Converting every database to a flat file
Disabling queries across sites
Reconciling differences among local schemas to provide a unified representation
questions.explanation: Schema integration resolves naming, structure and representation differences among participating databases.

questions.q: What is a distributed database catalog?
options: Metadata describing distributed data, schemas, locations and related information
A list of web browser bookmarks
A transaction that updates every row
A physical network cable
questions.explanation: A catalog helps the distributed DBMS locate data and understand the schemas and placement of distributed objects.

questions.q: What is the CAP theorem commonly used to discuss?
options: The syntax of SQL joins
Trade-offs among consistency, availability and partition tolerance in distributed systems
B-tree node capacity
The difference between DDL and DML
questions.explanation: CAP describes limits on simultaneously guaranteeing consistency and availability when a network partition occurs.
